summary: Gives definitions and an overview of the System for Cross-domain Identity Management (SCIM). It lays out the concepts, models and flows, and includes user scenarios, use cases and requirements for managing user identities across systems.

plainLanguage.summary: Moving to a new school means filling out the same forms. SCIM is a shared way for computer systems to pass around who people are.

questions: what is identity management in the cloud
subtitle: Moving user accounts between cloud services with a standard format.

tldr.problem: When users change cloud services or an organization needs accounts in multiple clouds, each service has its own user format and API, making integration expensive and error-prone.
tldr.mechanism: SCIM defines a standard schema for representing users and their attributes, plus scenarios and use cases for provisioning, de-provisioning and updating those identities across services.
tldr.outcome: Organizations can move users between cloud providers and services without reformatting their data, reducing integration cost and complexity.

facts.label: Main trigger types
facts.value: Create, Update, Delete, SSO, Password Reset

today: RFC 7642 is an Informational RFC that defines the concepts and requirements for user identity management across cloud systems. It has not been obsoleted and works together with RFC 7643 (schema) and RFC 7644 (protocol) to form the complete SCIM specification.

sections.title: What SCIM Solves
sections.content:
The System for Cross-domain Identity Management (SCIM) specification aims to make it fast, cheap, and easy to move users into, out of, and around the cloud. It defines a standard user schema and extension model for representing identity information, along with standard ways to exchange this data between systems.

Unlike SAML2 WebSSO and other federation approaches that focus on authentication, SCIM separates provisioning (creating and managing user accounts) from authentication. This allows systems to set up accounts before a user logs in (just-in-time provisioning) or to manage accounts in advance.
sections.plainLanguage: SCIM is about moving and managing user information between systems. It is not about logging in; it is about making sure the right user information is in the right place.

sections.title: Key Concepts and Actors
sections.content:
SCIM scenarios involve three kinds of actors: a Cloud Service Provider (CSP, the service that holds the user's account), an Enterprise Cloud Subscriber (ECS, a company that buys the service for its employees), and a Cloud Service User (CSU, the actual end user). A trigger starts a flow: create, update, delete, or a special case like single sign-on.

Data flows in two modes: Push (one system sends data to another) or Pull (one system requests data from another). Common flows are Cloud-to-Cloud (CSP to CSP), where two cloud services exchange user accounts, and Enterprise-to-Cloud (ECS to CSP), where a company pushes its employees' data to a cloud service.
sections.plainLanguage: There are three kinds of things: the cloud service that holds the account (CSP), the company using that service (ECS), and the person with the account (CSU). Data flows in two directions: push (sending) and pull (asking for).

sections.title: Use Cases: Identity Migration, SSO, and Provisioning
sections.content:
A migration scenario happens when a company moves its employee identities from one cloud provider to another without changing how the identities are stored. A single sign-on (SSO) scenario occurs when two cloud providers trust each other and one creates a user account based on authentication from the other. A provisioning scenario happens when an organization (like an HR service) distributes employee accounts to multiple systems across the world, including private and public clouds.

SCIM also handles change notifications: when a user's status changes (moved to a new department, left the company), one system tells another. All scenarios assume the systems involved support a common standard for user representation and identity operations.
sections.plainLanguage: SCIM handles: moving accounts between clouds, creating accounts when someone logs in, distributing accounts to lots of systems, and telling systems when user info changes.

sections.title: Flows and Operations
sections.content:
The document outlines six flow types between cloud providers: Create Identity (a new user joins), Update Identity (a user changes attributes like department), Delete Identity (a user leaves), SSO Trigger (Push) (one provider sends an account during login), SSO Trigger (Pull) (another provider requests account data during login), and Password Reset (changing a password in one system).

The same flow types apply between an enterprise and a cloud service. The difference is the actors: two cloud services on equal footing exchange accounts, while an enterprise initiates changes to its service provider's accounts. All flows use CRUD (Create, Read, Update, Delete) operations at the protocol level.
sections.plainLanguage: The main operations are: create a user, change a user, delete a user, and tell another system about these changes.

sections.title: Requirements and Security
sections.content:
All scenarios require that participating systems support a common identity schema and protocol for managing that schema. Systems must authenticate each other and ensure all identity operations are protected from unauthorized access and eavesdropping. Audit logging is required: changes to identity information must be logged, the logs must be secure, and they must be available for auditing.

When identities cross regulatory boundaries (between different countries or states with different privacy laws), cloud providers must ensure compliance. This RFC outlines the requirements; the actual protocol and schema are defined in RFC 7643 (schema) and RFC 7644 (protocol).
sections.plainLanguage: Systems must talk securely to each other, log all changes, and follow the laws of every country where user data lives.
